newsitem.title: USA: FDA has some authority over tobacco - U.S. judge.
newsitem.headline: FDA has some authority over tobacco - U.S. judge.

text.p: A federal judge ruled Friday that the Food and Drug Administration can regulate sales and labeling on cigarettes but cannot regulate the promotion and advertising of tobacco products.

The ruling by U.S. District Court Judge William Osteen appeared to be a mixed one for the tobacco industry and anti-smoking forces. The U.S. tobacco industry had challenged as unconstitutional new curbs on advertising and marketing of cigarettes imposed by federal regulators.

Osteen heard arguments in February that the FDA had overstepped its authority and was violating U.S. free-speech guarantees with its new rules limiting the sale and advertising of cigarettes. His ruling may be appealed.
The ruling comes as cigarette makers are under growing pressure to settle lawsuits seeking billions of dollars for smoking-related illness.
The Clinton administration said it would appeal Osteen's ruling that the FDA cannot regulate the advertising and promotion of tobacco.
Tobacco stocks fell after the ruling, which traders said was mixed but more negative for cigarette makers.

Philip Morris, the world's largest tobacco company, fell $2 to $39.625, RJR Nabisco Holdings lost $1.50 to $30.125 and Loews Corp., which owns Lorillard, dropped $1.375 to $90.75, all on the New York Stock Exchange.
"We're hearing it's a mixed ruling, but more on the downside," said Paul Diamond, a trader at Bankers Trust.
The regulatory battle dates back to August 1995, when President Bill Clinton authorised the FDA to regulate how cigarettes are sold and marketed in a bid to curb smoking by children.

The FDA rules would ban free samples and billboard ads near schools and playgrounds, limit vending machine sales and ban tobacco sponsorship of sports events and the use of cigarette brands on hats, T-shirts and other products.

The rules would also restrict ads in some publications and require retailers to see photo identification for cigarette purchasers under age 27. Some of the rules took effect in February and others were to take effect later this year.

In ruling that the FDA can regulate cigarette sales, the judge wrote: "The legislative history's silence regarding tobacco products does not indicate that Congress clearly intended to exempt such products from the act."
He was referring to the Food, Drug and Cosmetics Act of 1938, which the tobacco industry contended the government had "tortured" to give itself authority over tobacco.
